Approaches with structural foundational models that did not perform better

Same data both times — 28,166 measured half-lives, 75 HLA alleles, all 9-mers — and the same question: does it rank peptides by stability better than what we already use?

Using peptide shape embedding

what Boltz-2 was asked to fold is shown above: the empty groove

  • 1Boltz-2 folds the HLA groove on its own
    the α1/α2 domain, 182 residues — no peptide in the fold
  • 2768-number pocket embedding
    the trunk representation, mean-pooled over the B and F pockets
  • 3one vector per allele
    75 vectors for 28,166 rows — frozen, and blind to the peptide
  • 4swapped in for the 34-residue pseudosequence
    same 60-unit network, same split, only the input block changes

Using confidence matrix

above: the native trimer, the 9-mer in amber, one residue drawn paler

  • 1Boltz-2 co-folds each peptide with its HLA
    native trimer, 382 tokens — 1,430 complexes, one fold each
  • 2read the model’s confidence in the pose
    per-residue pLDDT · PAE to the pockets · ipTM
  • 339 numbers per complex
    peptide-specific by construction; no label read before folding
  • 4rank peptides, or train on the 39
    zero-shot ranking within an allele, or gradient boosting / the baseline net

Cartoons spin from 1M6O (HLA-B*44:02 + 9-mer), an experimental structure from the repo — nothing on this slide is predicted.

Both lose to the encoding we already use

  • Shape embedding — 768 learned dimensions land 0.04 below a substitution matrix, and every other embedding arm was worse.
  • Confidence matrix — the signal is real (p = 5×10−5, positive in 48 of 67 alleles) and about a third of what you get by ignoring the HLA entirely.

The confidence route was scored leave-one-allele-out, the easier split — so 0.11 is the optimistic reading. Press ↓ for the full arm tables.
